extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, bibliometricians, research administrators, and sociologists of science interested in citation analysis and research evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical-methods for assessing the use and validity of citation counts as indicators of scholarly contribution, and methodological standards for surveying scientists about those uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis 1 — effect of individual citation level
rubrics_metrics.description: "Scientists who are highly cited will be more likely to use citation counts for gauging scholarly contributions than will infrequently cited scientists. The former will also evaluate citation counts for this purpose more highly than the latter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of citation counts should account for the scientist’s own citation level: highly-cited researchers are more likely to (a) use citation counts and (b) regard them as valid measures; conversely, infrequently cited researchers may regard counts less favorably. Use this when analyzing attitudes or validity claims about citation metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis 2a — field consensus affects use
rubrics_metrics.description: "Scientists in fields with relatively low levels of consensus on appropriate research questions and techniques will be more likely to use citation counts to measure individuals’ scholarly contributions than scientists in fields with relatively high levels of consensus. The former will also evaluate such use of citation counts more favorably than the latter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying citation counts as indicators across disciplines, account for disciplinary 'consensus' (codification, norms, methods). Low-consensus fields (e.g., some social sciences) may rely on citation counts more; high-consensus fields (e.g., many natural sciences) may rely less because shared evaluative standards already exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis 2b — interaction of individual citation level and field consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: "The relationship between one’s own citation level and one’s use of citation counts to measure scholarly contributions will be stronger in fields with less consensus than in fields with more consensus. Similarly, the relation between one’s own citation level and one’s evaluation of citation counts as a measure should be stronger in lower-consensus fields."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect the partisan effect of personal citation standing (Hypothesis 1) to be magnified in low-consensus disciplines; analyses of metric validity should test for field × individual citation interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis on methodological orientation within a field
rubrics_metrics.description: "Among sociologists, those primarily interested in quantitative research areas will use and favor citation counts more than those with primarily qualitative or theoretical interests."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitudes toward citation metrics vary by subfield methodological orientation; surveys or evaluations should measure and control for respondents’ methodological specialization (quantitative vs qualitative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about quantitative data as independent predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: "Those who doubt the value of quantitative data generally should have a low opinion of citation counts quite apart from other factors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate general epistemic attitudes toward quantitative evidence from social-comparison explanations when assessing opinions about citation counts; include measures of methodological skepticism in analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat — quantitative measures can distort scholarly behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: "Widespread use of publication counts as a basis for promotion decisions is sometimes blamed for a deluge of trivial publications...using one or two easily quantifiable aspects to assess a scientist’s scholarly product tends to debase that product."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use citation counts cautiously in personnel decisions: be aware of perverse incentives (salami-slicing, trivial publications) and the risk that over-reliance on single numeric indicators will degrade research quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish purposes: bibliographic retrieval vs evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey finding: respondents reported using the Science Citation Index primarily for information retrieval, though respondents also noted that it is used for tenure evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between citation indexes’ roles (information retrieval, literature tracing) and their roles as evaluative metrics (tenure, hiring); evidence of use for retrieval does not imply endorsement as a fair evaluative measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: SCI as a quick bibliographic purview
rubrics_metrics.description: "The SCI is invaluable for providing a quick bibliographic purview and impression of a scientist’s work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat citation indexes as efficient tools for obtaining an overview of a scholar’s publications and citation footprint; useful for initial assessments but not sufficient alone for nuanced evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire design: brevity and format
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors designed a very brief questionnaire 'to fit on a postcard' and expected higher response rates because of its brevity. They also mailed follow-up questionnaires three weeks later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When surveying busy academics about bibliometric attitudes, keep instruments extremely brief (postcard length), and plan timely follow-ups to increase response rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling frame: choose strata by discipline and department prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Samples were drawn from graduate faculty lists for biochemistry and sociology and stratified by high- and low-prestige departments (Jones et al. 1982 rankings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To study cross-field differences in attitudes toward metrics, stratify sampling by discipline and institutional prestige to capture variation related to departmental reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target population & exclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The study sought associate and full professors, excluding ranks below associate and professors emeriti because low citation levels often reflect professional youth or retirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit sampling to career-stage cohorts for whom citation measures are comparable (e.g., associate/full professors) to avoid confounding by career age; explicitly state and justify exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling fraction and within-department limits
rubrics_metrics.description: They included no more than one-third of the members of any one department in the sample to avoid overrepresentation, and computed required departmental counts to reach targeted sample sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cap per-department sampling fractions to avoid clustering bias; compute sampling frames to reach desired absolute counts per stratum (e.g., 50 associate/full professors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect biographical and bibliometric covariates
rubrics_metrics.description: Collected sex, academic rank, year of Ph.D., number of citations in the 1984 SCI (or SSCI), and the median citations for the sample member’s department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather demographic and bibliometric covariates to control for confounders when analyzing attitudes about citation counts and to assess relative standing within departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect respondent confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: After gathering data, "we worked only with identification numbers to protect our respondents’ confidentiality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De-identify survey and bibliometric data during analysis and reporting; use ID numbers rather than names when storing and analyzing sensitive information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizing methodological orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: For the sociology sample the authors constructed a measure of whether a respondent is likely to view quantitative analysis favorably by classifying listed specialties from the 1985 Guide to Graduate Departments into quantitative, nonquantitative, or mixed categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize subfield methodological orientation via self-reported or directory-listed specialties, and validate classification (resolve discrepant codings) before analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use year-specific citation counts and departmental medians
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliometric data used were counts of citations in the 1984 SCI/SSCI and department medians to assess relative eminence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use time-bounded citation windows and department-level medians when evaluating individual citation standing to provide temporal and local context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for response bias and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The study notes that eminent scholars are slightly underrepresented in responses and that members of high-ranked departments were less likely to return questionnaires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and adjust for response bias by comparing respondent demographics/metrics to the sampling frame; report response rates by stratum and consider weighting or sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical framework: social comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Festinger’s social comparison theory (and attribution integration) to explain why individuals seek objective measures and how citation counts can validate self-evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting attitudes toward citation metrics, use social comparison theory: lack of objective benchmarks increases reliance on comparative, quantifiable indicators; explicitly link empirical hypotheses to theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct validation interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Discovering one’s work is highly cited confirms positive self-evaluations and at the same time validates citation counts as a measure of scholarly contribution. This is a kind of construct validation..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat citation counts’ agreement with self-evaluation or peer recognition as a form of construct validation, but test alternative explanations (e.g., field practices, publication norms) and avoid tautological inferences.
